title: Hiking Route Planner with Elevation
description: Plan a hike with distance, total climb and two time estimates — the router's and Naismith's rule — with the Hiking Route Planner with Elevation. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 10-mile route with 2,000 ft of climb prices out at about 4 hours 20 minutes by Naismith's rule — the estimate a century of hill walkers have planned by.
quick_answer: The Hiking Route Planner with Elevation builds a route from trailhead, waypoints and finish, then reports distance, total climb from terrain data, and two time estimates side by side: the routing engine's and the classic Naismith rule. Compare them and plan on the one your legs have validated.
steps_intro: A hike is distance plus climb plus honesty about both. Plan all three:

body.t: Distance alone lies about mountain days. Distance + climb + Naismith is the plan experienced walkers actually make — then the
A route's climb total is the figure that decides whether the group finishes together. See it before the car park, not at the steep bit.
Each day's leg gets the same treatment: routed path, climb, two times. The trek becomes a chain of honest days.
Short days punish optimistic estimates. Naismith plus a headtorch margin is the winter rule this planner makes easy to obey.
10 miles, 2,000 ft of ascent: flat time at 3 mph = 3 h 20 min; climb allowance = 30 min per 1,000 ft = 1 h; total ≈ 4 h 20 min. The formula is from 1892 and still embarrasses optimistic apps.
15 km with 800 m of climb: 15 ÷ 5 km/h = 3 h, plus 800 m at 30 min per 300 m ≈ 1 h 20 min → ≈ 4 h 20 min. Different hills, same honest arithmetic.

popular_table.title: Naismith's rule, tabulated
popular_table.intro: Time = distance at 3 mph (5 km/h) + 30 minutes per 1,000 ft (approx. 300 m) of ascent. Descents, rests and weather are yours to add.
popular_table.note: Naismith assumed a fit walker on decent ground. Your measured pace from the pace calculator is the correction your plans deserve.

faq: What is Naismith's rule?

William Naismith's 1892 rule of thumb: allow one hour for every 3 miles (5 km) forward, plus half an hour for every 1,000 ft (300 m) of ascent. This planner shows its estimate beside the router's so you can judge both.
Which time should I trust?
The one your own history validates. Walk a known route, compare both estimates with your actual time, and plan with the winner — the tools give you the comparison.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Trails have conditions instead of traffic; neither estimate knows about today's mud, snow or your knee.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Trails wind further still. The planner routes on the trail network's data, which is the distance your legs will meet.
Can route results change over time?
Paths are re-routed and terrain data improves; re-plan a route rather than trusting last year's export.
Where does the climb figure come from?
Terrain (elevation) data sampled along the routed path, summed over its rises. It is a model of the hill, not a survey of it.
Does descent cost time?
Naismith's original rule ignores gentle descents and modern walkers often add a little for steep ones. The estimates shown keep the classic form so they stay comparable.
Can I add a summit or a pub as a waypoint?
Yes — any point on the way becomes a waypoint, and the totals re-plan around your priorities, sacred or otherwise.
The router's time is much lower than Naismith's.
Routers assume steady movement on mapped paths; Naismith prices the climbing. On flat routes they converge; in the hills the gap is the lesson.
What if a path is missing from the data?
The router cannot use what the open map does not know. Local knowledge and recent guidebooks outrank any planner where they disagree.
